sources.entry: A wiki is a publication collaboratively edited and managed by its own audience directly using a web browser.

summary.name: Wiki
summary.one_liner: A wiki is a hypertext publication on the internet that its audience collaboratively edits and manages directly through a web browser, powered by wiki software (wiki engines).
use_cases: Building a shared knowledge base or documentation site
Creating a community or local city wiki
Organizing research or team information with edit history
summary.what_it_does: The page explains wikis as browser-editable publications whose pages anyone (or a defined group) can edit and link together. Wiki engines support source editing with lightweight markup, and some add visual rich-text editors. Most keep version history, allow reverting edits, show recent changes and diffs, and offer title search, with some providing full-text search. The page also covers access control levels, watchlists, patrolled revisions, and anti-vandalism measures such as bots. Wikis can be run as scripts on a web server, standalone application servers, personal single-computer installs, or on wiki farms.
notable: First wiki, WikiWikiWeb, launched by Ward Cunningham in 1995; the name comes from the Hawaiian word for 'quick'
Wikis use soft security: easy correction of mistakes via version history rather than prevention
Wiki engines are available both free/open-source and proprietary; MediaWiki powers Wikipedia
caveats: Free wiki farms typically display advertising on every page, and some hosted wikis are paid or private.
Open editing invites trolling, cybervandalism, and edit wars, which may go unnoticed for long periods on large wikis.
Public wikis can raise copyright and liability questions depending on licensing and jurisdiction.
